title: A Prayer From the Edge
overview: A worn-out person cries to God for safety, longs to stay close to God, prays for the king's long life, and promises lifelong praise.

parts.label: A cry from far off (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The writer calls to God from the far edge of the earth, which may mean literally far from home and the place of worship, or simply feeling at the very limit of what they can bear. They ask to be led to a rock that is higher than I, a safe high place they cannot climb to alone, and lean on the fact that God has protected them before like a strong tower.

parts.label: Longing to stay near God (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: The writer wants to live for good in God's sacred tent, the place where Israel worshiped, and to hide under the cover of God's wings, a picture of a bird sheltering its young. Vows were solemn promises made to God in prayer, and the writer trusts that God heard them and gave him a share in what belongs to people who honor God.

parts.label: A prayer for the king (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: The psalm turns to the king's long life and secure rule; if David wrote it, as the heading says, he may be speaking of himself, though it may also be a prayer offered for a king. God's love and faithfulness are pictured like two guards set to protect him, and Christians later read the word forever here as pointing to Jesus as the lasting king.

parts.label: A promise to keep singing (v. 8)
parts.note: The writer ends by promising to praise God and keep those vows day after day. The help they hope for is meant to turn into a lasting habit of thanks.

disagreement: Readers differ on who the king in verses 6 and 7 is: David speaking of himself, a later king of Israel prayed for by the people, or, as many Christians read it, ultimately the Messiah.
think: When you have felt worn down or far from everything familiar, what, if anything, felt like solid ground you could not have reached on your own?
